planting.note: Set divisions at their original depth in early spring into permanently damp, nutrient-poor meadow or bog-margin soil; avoid rich garden beds, which favor foliage over the dense purple-spotted flower spikes.

directions: This widespread European meadow and fen orchid produces compact spikes of magenta to purple flowers in late spring, usually shorter and earlier-blooming than the related southern and common marsh orchids. It thrives where groundwater keeps the soil consistently damp through the growing season but the crown is never left in stagnant standing water, such as a lean wet-meadow mix or pond-margin planting with coarse grit added to clay. Clumps slowly bulk up from annually renewed tuberoids and resent disturbance, so divide sparingly, only every four to five years, immediately after flowering finishes. Underplant with low, non-competitive grasses or sedges to mimic the open hay-meadow conditions it needs to persist long term.

planting.note: Repot the pseudobulbs every January into a free-draining bark, grit, and leaf-mold mix in a shallow pan; keep bone-dry and cold through winter rest, then resume watering as the flower buds emerge ahead of the new leaf.

directions: One of the best-known Ian Butterfield hybrid grexes, this Pleione bears large apricot-yellow flowers with a frilled, maroon-flecked lip ahead of its single pleated leaf each spring, and its unusual color and reliability earned it a long-standing RHS Award of Garden Merit. Pseudobulbs are typically grown in shallow terracotta pans under cold-frame or alpine-house protection, moved outdoors to a shaded, sheltered spot once the leaf is fully expanded for the summer growing season. Feed lightly through summer, withhold water completely as the leaf yellows in autumn, and keep the dormant pseudobulbs cold and dry until new growth resumes. Where winters stay reliably above the mid-teens Fahrenheit it can be bedded in a raised, humus-rich shaded trough, but most growers treat it as a protected container alpine.

planting.note: Repot pseudobulbs annually in midwinter into a free-draining bark, grit, and leaf-mold mix set in a shallow pan; keep cold and completely dry during winter dormancy and water only after flower buds appear.

directions: Another widely grown Butterfield grex, this Pleione produces broad, rounded mauve-pink flowers with a deeply fringed, maroon-blotched lip and is counted among the easiest and showiest hybrids for beginning growers of hardy pseudobulbous orchids. Grow it exactly as other windowsill and alpine-house Pleione: shallow pans of bark, grit, and leaf mold, a shaded bright spot through the growing season, regular dilute feeding while the leaf is active, and a hard dry winter rest once the leaf withers. Divide the clustering pseudobulbs when repotting each year, discarding any that are shriveled or diseased, and keep young offsets slightly drier until they establish their own roots. In mild, humid climates it can be trialed in a sheltered shaded trough outdoors, but container culture under glass remains the standard approach.
